record.paper_title: Discrepancy estimates for sequences: new results and open problems
record.original_question: Work out in detail the program sketched in the paper for using hybrid sequences in the J.P. Morgan Credit Metrics credit-risk simulation system: choose a dimension s<d for which an s-dimensional low-discrepancy sequence with N points is preferable to pseudorandom simulation, identify the s credits contributing most to portfolio risk, run the Credit Metrics simulation using quasi-Monte Carlo coordinates for those high-risk credits and pseudorandom coordinates for the remaining credits, and analyze the resulting performance against pure Monte Carlo and pure quasi-Monte Carlo methods.

evidence.quote: Open Problem 15 Carry out the above sketched program for using hybrid sequences in the credit risk management program Credit Metrics in detail and analyse the performance in comparison with pure Monte Carlo or pure quasi-Monte Carlo methods.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider the J.P. Morgan Credit Metrics credit-risk simulation framework for a portfolio of d obligors (credits). In a standard Monte Carlo implementation, each simulation trial requires sampling a d-dimensional vector of latent variables (e.g., correlated Gaussian factors driving asset returns) used to determine, for each obligor, whether a credit-rating migration or default occurs over the risk horizon, and to compute the resulting portfolio loss distribution and risk measures such as Value at Risk and Expected Shortfall.

A hybrid sequence in [0,1)^d is a sequence of points whose coordinates are split into two blocks: an s-dimensional block (s < d) taken from a low-discrepancy sequence (a quasi-Monte Carlo sequence such as a Halton, Sobol' or (t,s)-sequence) and a (d−s)-dimensional block taken from a pseudorandom sequence. After applying coordinate-wise transformations (e.g., the inverse Gaussian CDF and a factor decomposition), this yields samples of the d-dimensional latent vector in which s coordinates are quasi-random and d−s coordinates are pseudorandom.

Problem. Carry out in full detail the following program and analyze it quantitatively.

(1) Determine, as a function of N (the number of simulation trials) and d, a threshold dimension s = s(N, d) < d up to which an s-dimensional low-discrepancy point set with N points is provably (or empirically) preferable to N pseudorandom points for integration of the relevant Credit Metrics payoff functionals.

(2) Specify and justify a procedure to identify the s obligors that contribute most to portfolio risk (for instance via marginal risk contributions, exposure-weighted default-probability ranking, or principal-component / factor-loading criteria), so that quasi-Monte Carlo coordinates are assigned to these high-risk credits and pseudorandom coordinates to the remaining d − s credits.

(3) Implement the Credit Metrics simulation with the resulting hybrid sequence and derive rigorous error/discrepancy bounds for the estimated loss-distribution functionals (mean loss, VaR at given confidence level, Expected Shortfall), exploiting available results on the discrepancy of hybrid sequences.

(4) Compare, both theoretically (in terms of asymptotic convergence rates and constants) and empirically (on representative portfolios), the performance of the hybrid method against (a) pure Monte Carlo simulation in dimension d and (b) pure quasi-Monte Carlo simulation in dimension d, identifying regimes of N, d, s and portfolio characteristics in which each method is superior.
artifact.category_tag: Hybrid quasi-Monte Carlo methods in credit risk
artifact.status_search_result: A 2014 study (Hybrid Monte Carlo-Methods in Credit Risk Management, arXiv:1405.1831, published in Monte Carlo Methods Appl. 2014) carries out the proposed program for Credit Metrics, comparing hybrid sequences against pure Monte Carlo and pure quasi-Monte Carlo, and reports that suitably chosen hybrid sequences in many relevant situations outperform both, and essentially never perform worse. Related work (Ren; Ökten and collaborators) also addresses QMC for credit portfolios. Thus the program is partially carried out, though a complete theoretical analysis covering all parameter regimes appears not fully settled.

status_evidence.title: Hybrid Monte Carlo-Methods in Credit Risk Management
status_evidence.snippet: Hybrid sequences used for simulations in Credit Metrics in many relevant situations perform better than pure Monte Carlo and pure quasi-Monte Carlo methods, and essentially never perform worse.
status_evidence.claim: The sketched program has been carried out in detail for Credit Metrics with comparative performance analysis.

status_evidence.title: Modeling and quasi-Monte Carlo simulation of risk in credit portfolios (Ren)
status_evidence.snippet: Quasi-random sequences introduced into credit portfolio models via Brownian bridge and PCA constructions substantially improve simulation effectiveness for VaR.
status_evidence.claim: Independent dissertation work supports the efficiency improvements of QMC-based methods over MC for credit risk simulation.
